q: As soon as I saw it I knew it was an omen; it means that you will remain powerful and that there will be no house in Ithaca more royal than your own.”

s: the suitors are wooers of Queen Penelope (attempting to take Ulysses’s place)
q: He is much the best man and the most persistent wooer, of all those who are paying court to my mother and trying to take Ulysses’ place.

s: the suitors are characterized by pride and insolence (extreme)
q: If you go near the suitors you will be undone to a certainty, for their pride and insolence reach the very heavens.

s: Phoenicians are mariners (cunning traders)
q: this place there came some cunning traders from Phoenicia (for the Phoenicians are great mariners) in a ship which they had freighted with gewgaws of all kinds

s: Phoenicians travels in a ship (freighted with gewgaws of all kinds)
q: this place there came some cunning traders from Phoenicia (for the Phoenicians are great mariners) in a ship which they had freighted with gewgaws of all kinds

s: Syra is a island (located above Ortygia)
q: You may have heard of an island called Syra that lies over above Ortygia,134 where the land begins to turn round and look in another direction

s: Syra has two communities (dividing the whole country)
q: It contains two communities, and the whole country is divided between these two.

s: Syra has fertile soil (suited to cattle and sheep)
q: It is not very thickly peopled, but the soil is good, with much pasture fit for cattle and sheep, and it abounds with wine and wheat.

s: Ulysses is master of Eumaeus (through Eumaeus’s service at the swine station)
q: but Jove has given you good as well as evil, for in spite of everything you have a good master, who sees that you always have enough to eat and drink;

s: Syra is ruled by Ctesius son of Ormenus (king of both communities)
q: My father Ctesius son of Ormenus, a man comparable to the gods, reigned over both.

s: Ithaca is the destination of Phoenician ship (after the abduction voyage)
q: Presently the winds and waves took the ship to Ithaca, where Laertes gave sundry of his chattels for me, and thus it was that ever I came to set eyes upon this country.”

s: the swineherd's hut houses Eumaeus (and his men)
q: Meanwhile Ulysses and the swineherd were eating their supper in the hut, and the men supped with them.

s: hospitality is provided by Piraeus son of Clytius (to Theoclymenus)
q: but I will look after him for you, and he shall find no lack of hospitality.”

s: hospitality is requested for Theoclymenus (by Telemachus)
q: I wish you would take this stranger to your own house and entertain him hospitably till I can come for him.”

s: hawk omen signifies Telemachus's power (according to Theoclymenus)
q: it means that you will remain powerful and that there will be no house in Ithaca more royal than your own.”

s: Ulysses is skilled as servant (claims exceptional versatility)
q: there is no one living who would make a more handy servant than I should—to put fresh wood on the fire, chop fuel, carve, cook, pour out wine, and do all those services that poor men have to do for their betters.”

s: Eumaeus is a swineherd (devoted servant of Ulysses)
q: where dwelt the excellent swineherd, who was so devoted a servant to his master.

s: Eumaeus is devoted to Ulysses (as a servant)
q: where dwelt the excellent swineherd, who was so devoted a servant to his master.

s: Eumaeus was raised with Ctimene (in Laertes’s household)
q: she brought me up along with her daughter Ctimene, the youngest of her children; we were boy and girl together, and she made little difference between us.

s: Ulysses is father of you
q: I am your father, on whose account you grieve and suffer so much at the hands of lawless men.

s: Telemachus is related to Ulysses (son and newly reunited with him)
q: As he spoke he kissed his son, and a tear fell from his cheek on to the ground

s: Telemachus is the only son of Ulysses (the sole heir in his family line)
q: I am myself the only son of Ulysses who left me behind him when he went away

s: Telemachus plans to hide the armour (in the strong store room)
q: you must collect all the armour that is in the house and hide it in the strong store room.

s: Telemachus keeps secret Ulysses's revelation to Telemachus (from the household and servants)
q: let no one know that Ulysses is within the house—neither Laertes, nor yet the swineherd, nor any of the servants, nor even Penelope herself.

s: Eumaeus is a swineherd (servant of Ulysses' household)
q: To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus

s: Eumaeus has station at the swineherd's station (where he keeps the pigs)
q: He says he is a Cretan, and that he has been a great traveller. At this moment he is running away from a Thesprotian ship, and has taken refuge at my station

s: Eumaeus heeds you
q: I understand and heed you,” replied Eumaeus; “you need instruct me no further

s: Penelope resides in house of Ulysses (still living there)
q: She is still at the house,” replied Eumaeus

s: Penelope grieves for Ulysses (continually, day and night)
q: grieving and breaking her heart, and doing nothing but weep, both night and day continually.

s: Penelope is wooed by the suitors (without yet choosing a husband)
q: the chiefs from all the neighbouring islands, Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, as also all the principal men of Ithaca itself, are eating up my house under the pretext of paying court to my mother

s: Ulysses is son of Laertes
q: Laertes was the only son of Arceisius, and Ulysses only son of Laertes.

s: Minerva is a goddess (redoubtable and able to change appearances)
q: What you wonder at is the work of the redoubtable goddess Minerva, who does with me whatever she will

s: Minerva possesses Minerva's golden wand (used to transform Ulysses' appearance)
q: As she spoke she touched him with her golden wand.

s: Minerva supports revenge upon the suitors (eager to join the fighting)
q: I will not be long in joining you, for I too am eager for the fray.

s: the suitors are wooing Penelope (while consuming Ulysses' household)
q: the chiefs from all the neighbouring islands, Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus, as also all the principal men of Ithaca itself, are eating up my house under the pretext of paying court to my mother

s: the suitors abuse house of Ulysses (wasting its goods and mistreating its people)
q: they are making havoc of my estate, and before long will do so with myself into the bargain.

s: the suitors number 108 (52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus, and 12 from Ithaca)
q: There are fifty-two chosen youths from Dulichium, and they have six servants; from Same there are twenty-four; twenty young Achaeans from Zacynthus, and twelve from Ithaca itself

s: the suitors have servants six (from Dulichium)
q: There are fifty-two chosen youths from Dulichium, and they have six servants

s: the suitors have with them servants, a bard, and carvers (household attendants at their banquets)
q: They have with them a servant Medon, a bard, and two men who can carve at table.

s: the armour is a armour (kept in the house of Ulysses)
q: you must collect all the armour that is in the house and hide it in the strong store room.

s: revenge upon the suitors is planned by Ulysses (in consultation with Telemachus)
q: I am now come here on the suggestion of Minerva that we may consult about killing our enemies.

s: Ulysses is father of Telemachus (absent father)
q: I am your father, on whose account you grieve and suffer so much at the hands of lawless men.

s: revenge upon the suitors is planned by Telemachus (with Ulysses)
q: I am now come here on the suggestion of Minerva that we may consult about killing our enemies.

s: the secret test of the household servants is planned by Ulysses (to identify loyal and disloyal servants)
q: Let you and me exploit the women alone, and let us also make trial of some other of the men servants, to see who is on our side and whose hand is against us.

s: the secret test of the household servants is supported by Telemachus (he accepts testing the women but postpones testing the men)
q: Prove the women by all means, to see who are disloyal and who guiltless, but I am not in favour of going round and trying the men.

s: Ulysses's revelation to Telemachus says I am your father
q: And Ulysses said, “I am no god, why should you take me for one? I am your father

s: Ulysses's return is enabled by Phaeacians (they transported him by sea while he slept)
q: It was the Phaeacians who brought me here. They are great sailors, and are in the habit of giving escorts to any one who reaches their coasts.

s: Ulysses has returned to Ithaca (after twenty years of wandering and hardship)
q: Such as I am, it is I, who after long wandering and much hardship have got home in the twentieth year to my own country.

s: Ulysses has treasure in Cave of the Naiads (concealed there after being brought to Ithaca)
q: They took me over the sea while I was fast asleep, and landed me in Ithaca, after giving me many presents in bronze, gold, and raiment. These things by heaven’s mercy are lying concealed in a cave

s: Ulysses is protected by Minerva (who can alter his appearance)
q: What you wonder at is the work of the redoubtable goddess Minerva, who does with me whatever she will, for she can do what she pleases.

s: Ulysses is disguised as beggar (when brought to the city)
q: Later on the swineherd will bring me to the city disguised as a miserable old beggar.

s: Telemachus is a son (only son of Ulysses)
q: I am myself the only son of Ulysses who left me behind him when he went away

s: Telemachus has returned from Pylos (safely returned)
q: tell Penelope that I am safe and have returned from Pylos.

s: Telemachus is a son (of Penelope and Ulysses)
q: Your son, Madam, is now returned from Pylos

s: Penelope is pursued by the suitors (in marriage)
q: you devour his property without paying for it, and break my heart by wooing his wife and trying to kill his son.

s: Penelope knows of the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus (through Medon's report)
q: She knew of the plot against Telemachus, for the servant Medon had overheard their counsels and had told her

s: Ulysses is a husband (of Penelope)
q: you devour his property without paying for it, and break my heart by wooing his wife and trying to kill his son.

s: Ulysses owns the estate of Ulysses
q: Then we can divide up his property amongst us

s: Ulysses has the house of Ulysses
q: and let his mother and the man who marries her have the house.

s: Ulysses protects Eupeithes (from the people of Ithaca)
q: They wanted to tear him in pieces and eat up everything he had, but Ulysses stayed their hands although they were infuriated

s: Antinous is a son of Eupeithes
q: Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke first.

s: Antinous is a schemer (insolent and wicked)
q: “Antinous, insolent and wicked schemer, they say you are the best speaker and counsellor of any man your own age in Ithaca

s: Antinous leads the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus
q: Let us try and lay hold of him either on his farm away from the town, or on the road hither.

s: Telemachus is a shrewd man
q: our affair is never likely to come off while he is alive, for he is very shrewd, and public feeling is by no means all on our side.

s: Eurymachus is a son of Polybus
q: Eurymachus, son of Polybus, was the first to speak.

s: Eurymachus is a plotter (against Telemachus)
q: He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.

s: Eurymachus claims friendship with Telemachus (deceptively)
q: Therefore Telemachus is much the dearest friend I have, and has nothing to fear from the hands of us suitors.

s: Amphinomus is a son of Nisus
q: He was the son of Nisus, who was son to king Aretias

s: Amphinomus is a suitor (foremost among the suitors from Dulichium)
q: and he was foremost among all the suitors from the wheat-growing and well grassed island of Dulichium

s: Amphinomus has good natural disposition
q: for he was a man of good natural disposition.

s: Amphinomus is favored by Penelope (in conversation)
q: his conversation, moreover, was more agreeable to Penelope than that of any of the other suitors

s: Amphinomus opposes killing Telemachus
q: I am not in favour of killing Telemachus. It is a heinous thing to kill one who is of noble blood.

s: the suitors are wooers (of Penelope)
q: you devour his property without paying for it, and break my heart by wooing his wife and trying to kill his son.

s: the suitors occupy the house of Ulysses (as customary guests and claimants)
q: Thus did he speak, and his words pleased them well, so they rose forthwith and went to the house of Ulysses, where they took their accustomed seats.

s: Telemachus undertakes Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon
q: this voyage of Telemachus’s is a very serious matter; we had made sure that it would come to nothing.

s: the suitors consume the estate of Ulysses (without paying for it)
q: you devour his property without paying for it

s: the suitors maintain the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus (to prevent him from summoning the Achaeans)
q: We must make haste before he can call the Achaeans in assembly

s: immortal gods control Telemachus's safety
q: Good heavens,” said he, “see how the gods have saved this man from destruction.

s: Minerva is a goddess
q: Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband till Minerva shed sleep over her eyes.

s: Minerva disguises Ulysses (as an old man)
q: Minerva therefore came up to Ulysses, turned him into an old man with a stroke of her wand, and clad him in his old clothes again

s: the ship is in the harbour (after returning from Pylos)
q: When they had come inside the harbour they drew the ship on to the land

s: the ship carries Telemachus's crew (from Pylos to Ithaca)
q: the ship which had brought Telemachus and his crew from Pylos had reached the town of Ithaca.

s: the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus is known by Penelope (through Medon)
q: She knew of the plot against Telemachus, for the servant Medon had overheard their counsels and had told her

s: marriage to Penelope is contingent on the suitors (the suitor offering the most)
q: she can marry the man who will give the most for her, and whose lot it is to win her.

s: Telemachus has the ship (sent back to Ithaca)
q: but had sent the ship to the town to prevent her from being alarmed and made unhappy.

s: Eumaeus is a swineherd
q: When he had given his message he left the house with its outbuildings and went back to his pigs again.

s: Eumaeus serves as messenger (for Telemachus)
q: but Eumaeus went close up to Penelope, and said privately all that her son had bidden him tell her.

s: Penelope is a daughter of Icarius
q: To this Eurymachus son of Polybus answered, “Take heart, Queen Penelope daughter of Icarius, and do not trouble yourself about these matters.

s: Ulysses is husband of Penelope
q: Madam, wife of Ulysses, Telemachus does not understand these things; listen therefore to me

s: Ulysses uses the beggar's wallet (carried over his shoulder)
q: As he spoke he threw his shabby old tattered wallet over his shoulders, by the cord from which it hung

s: Ulysses uses the staff (to walk on the rough road)
q: Let us be going, but if you have a stick ready cut, let me have it to walk with, for you say the road is a very rough one.

s: Ulysses endures begging and hunger (as a hardship common to human beings)
q: But a man cannot hide away the cravings of a hungry belly; this is an enemy which gives much trouble to all men

s: Ulysses prepares revenge upon the suitors (while concealed in Ithaca)
q: Ulysses himself is even now in Ithaca, and, either going about the country or staying in one place, is enquiring into all these evil deeds and preparing a day of reckoning for the suitors.

s: Eumaeus is a swineherd (servant of Ulysses)
q: “Old friend,” said he to the swineherd
